## 10. Setup time and environment notes

- No Docker on the development machine, so the hosted path (README Path B) is the only one used.
- The machine had Node 20; Expo SDK 58 (the SDK current Expo Go runs) requires Node ≥ 22.13. A
  portable Node 22 was downloaded (SHA-256 verified) into the git-ignored `.tools/` folder rather
  than changing the system install.
- Offline verification uses PGlite (Postgres 17 compiled to WASM) with a small Supabase shim
  (`server/test/support/supabase-shim.sql`: the API roles, the `auth` tables the seed writes, and
  Supabase's default grants, so the migrations' revokes are exercised). It is a faithful Postgres,
  not Supabase: Auth, PostgREST and the pooler are only covered by the hosted suite.

## 11. Known limitations and remaining risks

See QA_REPORT.md for the verification status of each item. Summarised:

- Hosted verification and the on-device run depend on a configured Supabase project and an
  emulator/device; their status is recorded in QA_REPORT.md as run, not assumed.
- No rate limiting on the API (out of scope here; would sit in front of Fastify).
- No pagination on meetup lists (groups are small; add keyset pagination on `(starts_at, id)`).
- The RSVP-vs-cancel race is covered on hosted Postgres only (PGlite is single-connection).

-- =====================================================================
-- Bonus work sample: authorization for the live walk Realtime channel.
--
-- Supabase Realtime Authorization checks RLS on realtime.messages when a
-- client joins a PRIVATE channel (select = receive, insert = send), with
-- realtime.topic() returning the channel name. Topic format:
--   meetup:<meetup uuid>:live
-- Live positions are as sensitive as the exact meeting point, so the
-- channel is open to exactly the people who may see that point (the
-- creator and attendees who are still members), and only while the meetup
-- is scheduled. Positions in the work sample are synthetic.
-- =====================================================================

create function app.live_walk_meetup_id(p_topic text)
returns uuid
language sql
immutable
set search_path = ''
as $$
  select case
    when p_topic ~ '^meetup:[0-9a-f]{8}-[0-9a-f]{4}-[0-9a-f]{4}-[0-9a-f]{4}-[0-9a-f]{12}:live$'
      then substring(p_topic from 8 for 36)::uuid
  end
$$;

create function app.can_join_live_walk(p_topic text)
returns boolean
language sql
stable
security definer
set search_path = ''
as $$
  select coalesce(
    app.can_see_exact_meeting_point(app.live_walk_meetup_id(p_topic))
    and exists (
      select 1 from public.meetups m
       where m.id = app.live_walk_meetup_id(p_topic) and m.status = 'scheduled'
    ),
    false
  )
$$;

-- =====================================================================
-- Bonus work sample: authorization for the live walk Realtime channel.
--
-- Supabase Realtime Authorization checks RLS on realtime.messages when a
-- client joins a PRIVATE channel (select = receive, insert = send), with
-- realtime.topic() returning the channel name. Topic format:
--   meetup:<meetup uuid>:live
-- Live positions are as sensitive as the exact meeting point, so the
-- channel is open to exactly the people who may see that point (the
-- creator and attendees who are still members), and only while the meetup
-- is scheduled. Positions in the work sample are synthetic.
-- =====================================================================

create function app.live_walk_meetup_id(p_topic text)
returns uuid
language sql
immutable
set search_path = ''
as $$
  select case
    when p_topic ~ '^meetup:[0-9a-f]{8}-[0-9a-f]{4}-[0-9a-f]{4}-[0-9a-f]{4}-[0-9a-f]{12}:live$'
      then substring(p_topic from 8 for 36)::uuid
  end
$$;

create function app.can_join_live_walk(p_topic text)
returns boolean
language sql
stable
security definer
set search_path = ''
as $$
  select coalesce(
    app.can_see_exact_meeting_point(app.live_walk_meetup_id(p_topic))
    and exists (
      select 1 from public.meetups m
       where m.id = app.live_walk_meetup_id(p_topic) and m.status = 'scheduled'
    ),
    false
  )
$$;

entries.name: Monitor
entries.description:
Start a background monitor that streams events from a long-running script. Each stdout line is an event — you keep working and notifications arrive in the chat. Events arrive on their own schedule and are not replies from the user, even if one lands while you're waiting for the user to answer a question.

Pick by how many notifications you need:
- **One** ("tell me when the server is ready / the build finishes") → use **Bash with `run_in_background`** and a command that exits when the condition is true, e.g. `until grep -q "Ready in" dev.log; do sleep 0.5; done`. You get a single completion notification when it exits.
- **One per occurrence, until the monitor expires (re-arm to continue)** ("tell me every time an ERROR line appears") → Monitor with an unbounded command (`tail -f`, `inotifywait -m`, `while true`).
- **One per occurrence, until a known end** ("emit each CI step result, stop when the run completes") → Monitor with a command that emits lines and then exits.

Your script's stdout is the event stream. Each line becomes a notification. Exit ends the watch.

  # Each matching log line is an event
  tail -f /var/log/app.log | grep --line-buffered "ERROR"

  # Each file change is an event
  inotifywait -m --format '%e %f' /watched/dir

  # Poll GitHub for new PR comments and emit one line per new comment
  last=$(date -u +%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ)
  while true; do
    now=$(date -u +%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ)
    gh api "repos/owner/repo/issues/123/comments?since=$last" --jq '.[] | "\(.user.login): \(.body)"'
    last=$now; sleep 30
  done

  # Node script that emits events as they arrive (e.g. WebSocket listener)
  node watch-for-events.js

  # Per-occurrence with a natural end: emit each CI check as it lands, exit when the run completes
  prev=""
  while true; do
    s=$(gh pr checks 123 --json name,bucket)
    cur=$(jq -r '.[] | select(.bucket!="pending") | "\(.name): \(.bucket)"' <<<"$s" | sort)
    comm -13 <(echo "$prev") <(echo "$cur")
    prev=$cur
    jq -e 'all(.bucket!="pending")' <<<"$s" >/dev/null && break
    sleep 30
  done

**Don't use an unbounded command for a single notification.** `tail -f`, `inotifywait -m`, and `while true` never exit on their own, so the monitor stays armed until timeout even after the event has fired. For "tell me when X is ready," use Bash `run_in_background` with an `until` loop instead (one notification, ends in seconds). Note that `tail -f log | grep -m 1 ...` does *not* fix this: if the log goes quiet after the match, `tail` never receives SIGPIPE and the pipeline hangs anyway.

**Script quality:**
- Every pipe stage must flush per line or matches sit in its buffer unseen: `grep` needs `--line-buffered`, `awk` needs `fflush()`. `head` cannot flush at all — `| head -N` delivers nothing until N matches accumulate, then ends the stream.
- In poll loops, handle transient failures (`curl ... || true`) — one failed request shouldn't kill the monitor.
- Poll intervals: 30s+ for remote APIs (rate limits), 0.5-1s for local checks.
- Write a specific `description` — it appears in every notification ("errors in deploy.log" not "watching logs").
- Only stdout is the event stream. Stderr goes to the output file (readable via Read) but does not trigger notifications — for a command you run directly (e.g. `python train.py 2>&1 | grep --line-buffered ...`), merge stderr with `2>&1` so its failures reach your filter. (No effect on `tail -f` of an existing log — that file only contains what its writer redirected.)

**Coverage — silence is not success.** When watching a job or process for an outcome, your filter must match every terminal state, not just the happy path. A monitor that greps only for the success marker stays silent through a crashloop, a hung process, or an unexpected exit — and silence looks identical to "still running." Before arming, ask: *if this process crashed right now, would my filter emit anything?* If not, widen it.

  # Wrong — silent on crash, hang, or any non-success exit
  tail -f run.log | grep --line-buffered "elapsed_steps="

  # Right — one alternation covering progress + the failure signatures you'd act on
  tail -f run.log | grep -E --line-buffered "elapsed_steps=|Traceback|Error|FAILED|assert|Killed|OOM"

For poll loops checking job state, emit on every terminal status (`succeeded|failed|cancelled|timeout`), not just success. If you cannot confidently enumerate the failure signatures, broaden the grep alternation rather than narrow it — some extra noise is better than missing a crashloop.

**Output volume**: Every stdout line is a conversation message, so the filter should be selective — but selective means "the lines you'd act on," not "only good news." Never pipe raw logs; filter to exactly the success and failure signals you care about. Monitors that produce too many events are automatically stopped; restart with a tighter filter if this happens.

Stdout lines within 200ms are batched into a single notification, so multiline output from a single event groups naturally.

The script runs in the same shell environment as Bash. Exit ends the watch (exit code is reported). Every monitor expires after `timeout_ms` (default 5 minutes, at most 30 minutes): it is killed and you get one notice with the event count. Re-arm it if you still need the watch; for a long watch (PR monitoring, log tails) set `timeout_ms` to the maximum and re-arm on each expiry, and widen the filter if an expiry with no events was unexpected. Use TaskStop to cancel early.
**ws source** — open a WebSocket and stream each incoming text frame as an event. No shell, no polling: the server pushes, you get notified.

  Monitor({
    ws: {url: 'wss://events.example.com/stream', protocols: ['v1']},
    description: 'deploy events',
  })

Each text frame becomes one notification (multiline frames stay as one event). Binary frames are reported as `[binary frame, N bytes]` rather than passed through. Socket close ends the watch with the close code surfaced; errors are surfaced before close. Same rate limiting as bash — a firehose will be suppressed and eventually stopped, so subscribe to a filtered feed where one exists.

Prefer this over `command: 'websocat wss://…'` — it avoids the extra process and line-buffering pitfalls. Use bash when you need to transform or filter frames with shell tools before they become events.

description.description: Short human-readable description of what you are monitoring (shown in notifications).

timeout_ms.description: Kill the monitor after this deadline. Default 300000ms. Deadlines above 1800000ms are capped to 1800000ms. You are notified at expiry and can re-arm.

command.description: Shell command or script. Each stdout line is an event; exit ends the watch.

ws.description: WebSocket to open. Each text frame is an event; binary frames are reported as a placeholder line. Socket close ends the watch. Cannot be combined with command.

The application is allowing me to edit meetups created by other users. This violates the official challenge requirements.

Investigate and fix this issue end to end.

1. Reproduce and identify the root cause

Inspect:

React Native meetup detail screen

Edit Meetup screen

User authentication and session state

Creator ID comparisons

Fastify update endpoint

Shared Zod schemas

Supabase database migrations

PostgreSQL RLS policies

Determine whether the problem is:

Edit button incorrectly visible

Edit screen accessible through navigation

Backend allowing unauthorized updates

RLS policy permitting updates by non-creators

Incorrect ownership detection

Inconsistent user IDs

Or multiple issues

Do not assume this is only a frontend problem.

2. Correct authorization

Only the original creator of a scheduled meetup may edit it.

Enforce:

meetup.creator_id must match the authenticated user's Supabase Auth ID.

The creator must be authorized for the meetup's group.

Cancelled meetups cannot be edited.

The client cannot modify creator_id or group_id.

A changed start time must be in the future.

Every update must pass through the Fastify endpoint and shared Zod validation.

Never trust an owner ID supplied by the mobile app.

3. Fix database security

Inspect the existing RLS policies.

Ensure PostgreSQL denies unauthorized updates by:

Other members of the same group

Members of unrelated groups

Outsiders

Ensure the authorized creator is permitted to update only the allowed fields.

Do not weaken existing SELECT, INSERT, DELETE, RSVP, cancellation, or location-privacy policies.

Check that no privileged database connection accidentally bypasses RLS.

Add a proper SQL migration if database policies need changes.

4. Fix React Native UI

Show the Edit Meetup action only when the signed-in user is the original creator.

Hide editing for cancelled meetups.

Block unauthorized navigation to Edit Meetup.

Handle backend 403 or 404 responses gracefully.

Keep the professional visual design consistent.

Do not use the frontend as the only security layer.

5. Add automated tests

Test with different seeded accounts:

Creator edits their own scheduled meetup — PASS.

Another member attempts to edit it — DENIED.

Outsider attempts to edit it — DENIED.

A user belonging to multiple groups attempts unauthorized editing — DENIED.

Creator attempts to edit a cancelled meetup — DENIED.

Creator changes start time to the past — DENIED.

Non-creator sends a direct HTTP update request — DENIED.

Non-creator attempts a direct database UPDATE — DENIED.

Creator attempts to change creator ID or group ID — DENIED.

Test actual hosted Supabase RLS, not only mocked API responses.

6. Regression QA

After fixing:

Run typecheck.

Run lint.

Run unit tests.

Run backend integration tests.

Run hosted RLS tests.

Verify the application on the Android emulator if available.

Recheck RSVP, withdrawal, cancellation, and map privacy.

Report the root cause, changed files, test evidence, and remaining limitations.

Do not claim tests passed without executing them.

The application is allowing me to edit meetups created by other users. This violates the official challenge requirements.

Investigate and fix this issue end to end.

1. Reproduce and identify the root cause

Inspect:

React Native meetup detail screen

Edit Meetup screen

User authentication and session state

Creator ID comparisons

Fastify update endpoint

Shared Zod schemas

Supabase database migrations

PostgreSQL RLS policies

Determine whether the problem is:

Edit button incorrectly visible

Edit screen accessible through navigation

Backend allowing unauthorized updates

RLS policy permitting updates by non-creators

Incorrect ownership detection

Inconsistent user IDs

Or multiple issues

Do not assume this is only a frontend problem.

2. Correct authorization

Only the original creator of a scheduled meetup may edit it.

Enforce:

meetup.creator_id must match the authenticated user's Supabase Auth ID.

The creator must be authorized for the meetup's group.

Cancelled meetups cannot be edited.

The client cannot modify creator_id or group_id.

A changed start time must be in the future.

Every update must pass through the Fastify endpoint and shared Zod validation.

Never trust an owner ID supplied by the mobile app.

3. Fix database security

Inspect the existing RLS policies.

Ensure PostgreSQL denies unauthorized updates by:

Other members of the same group

Members of unrelated groups

Outsiders

Ensure the authorized creator is permitted to update only the allowed fields.

Do not weaken existing SELECT, INSERT, DELETE, RSVP, cancellation, or location-privacy policies.

Check that no privileged database connection accidentally bypasses RLS.

Add a proper SQL migration if database policies need changes.

4. Fix React Native UI

Show the Edit Meetup action only when the signed-in user is the original creator.

Hide editing for cancelled meetups.

Block unauthorized navigation to Edit Meetup.

Handle backend 403 or 404 responses gracefully.

Keep the professional visual design consistent.

Do not use the frontend as the only security layer.

5. Add automated tests

Test with different seeded accounts:

Creator edits their own scheduled meetup — PASS.

Another member attempts to edit it — DENIED.

Outsider attempts to edit it — DENIED.

A user belonging to multiple groups attempts unauthorized editing — DENIED.

Creator attempts to edit a cancelled meetup — DENIED.

Creator changes start time to the past — DENIED.

Non-creator sends a direct HTTP update request — DENIED.

Non-creator attempts a direct database UPDATE — DENIED.

Creator attempts to change creator ID or group ID — DENIED.

Test actual hosted Supabase RLS, not only mocked API responses.

6. Regression QA

After fixing:

Run typecheck.

Run lint.

Run unit tests.

Run backend integration tests.

Run hosted RLS tests.

Verify the application on the Android emulator if available.

Recheck RSVP, withdrawal, cancellation, and map privacy.

Report the root cause, changed files, test evidence, and remaining limitations.

Do not claim tests passed without executing them.
</pasted_content id="a4f1">

test(hosted): prove creator-only editing in the hosted database, not only via the API

Prompted by a report that a non-creator could edit a meetup. Investigation
on the hosted project: the Saturday loop's meeting point had been changed,
but as altair_api_writer only the creator (Avery) can update it; Jordan,
Sam, Riley (both groups), Quinn and Taylor change 0 rows. The app only
shows Edit when viewer.canEdit (creator + scheduled) and the API returns
403/404 otherwise, so no authorization defect was found.

The real gap was coverage: hosted tests checked edit authorization only
through the API, whose own 403 would mask a database hole. New hosted tests:
non-creators (same group, multi-group, other group, outsider) change 0 rows;
the creator cannot change group, creator, or start in the past (42501/AL006);
cancelled meetups cannot be edited (AL004); PostgREST edits are refused (42501).

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

# DOCX creation, editing, and analysis

If you are about to make a new document and this session offers Claude's own docs (a Docs connector, docs skill or Docs artifact type), and the user has neither named Word/.docx/.dotx, asked for tracked changes, nor supplied a .docx/.dotx file to change or use as a template, make the document there instead. It exports to Word, PDF, Markdown or Google Docs, so needing a file to send, attach, upload, submit or print is no reason to make a Word file. A .docx/.dotx given only as source material does not count as supplied. This skill remains the right tool for producing, reading, editing, templating or converting Word files.

A `.docx` is a ZIP archive of XML files. Choose your approach by task:

| Task | Approach |
|---|---|
| **Create** a new document | Write a `docx` (npm) script — see gotchas below |
| **Edit** an existing document | `unzip` → edit `word/document.xml` → `zip` (docx-js cannot open existing files) |
| **Read** content | `pandoc -t markdown file.docx` |

> Script paths below are relative to this skill's directory.

## Creating with docx-js — gotchas

`docx` is preinstalled — do not run `npm install` first; write the script and `require('docx')` directly. Only if that require fails: `npm install docx`. The model knows the API; these are the footguns:

- **Page size defaults to A4.** For US Letter set `page: { size: { width: 12240, height: 15840 } }` (DXA; 1440 = 1″).
- **Landscape:** pass portrait dimensions and `orientation: PageOrientation.LANDSCAPE` — docx-js swaps width/height internally.
- **Tables need dual widths:** set `columnWidths` on the table AND `width` on every cell, both in `WidthType.DXA` (PERCENTAGE breaks in Google Docs). Column widths must sum to the table width.
- **Table shading:** use `ShadingType.CLEAR`, never `SOLID` (renders black).
- **Lists:** never insert `•` literally; use a `numbering` config with `LevelFormat.BULLET`.
- **`ImageRun` requires `type:`** (`"png"`, `"jpg"`, …).
- **`PageBreak` must be inside a `Paragraph`.**
- **Never use `\n`** — use separate `Paragraph` elements.
- **TOC:** headings must use built-in `HeadingLevel.*`; custom heading styles need `outlineLevel` set or they won't appear.
- **Don't use a table as a horizontal rule** — use a paragraph bottom border instead.
- **Dot-leader / right-aligned-on-same-line:** use `PositionalTab` (`alignment: PositionalTabAlignment.RIGHT`, `leader: PositionalTabLeader.DOT`) inside a `TextRun`, not literal `.` or space padding.

## Verify the output

After writing a `.docx`, render it and look at it:

```bash
python scripts/office/soffice.py --headless --convert-to pdf output.docx
pdftoppm -jpeg -r 100 output.pdf page
ls page-*.jpg   # then Read the images
```

`pdftoppm` zero-pads page numbers to the width of the page count (`page-01.jpg`…`page-12.jpg`).

## Editing existing documents

Legacy `.doc` files must be converted first: `python scripts/office/soffice.py --headless --convert-to docx file.doc`.

```bash
unzip -q doc.docx -d unpacked/
find unpacked -type l -delete   # strip symlink entries — docx from external parties is untrusted
python scripts/merge_runs.py unpacked/   # coalesce fragmented runs so text is findable
# edit unpacked/word/document.xml in place — do NOT reformat or pretty-print
(cd unpacked && rm -f ../out.docx && zip -Xr ../out.docx .)
python scripts/office/validate.py out.docx --original doc.docx   # XSD checks; --auto-repair fixes common issues
# redlining? add --author "<the name you redlined under>" to check every edit is tracked
```

Word splits text across many `<w:r>` runs (revision ids, spell-check markers), so a phrase you can see in the document often doesn't exist as a contiguous string in the XML. `merge_runs.py` merges adjacent identically-formatted runs in `word/document.xml` without changing content or rendering; it also accepts a `.docx` directly (`python scripts/merge_runs.py doc.docx -o merged.docx`).

**Tracked changes:** when redlining, validate with `--author "<the name you redlined under>"` (needs `--original`) — it reports any text you changed without a `<w:ins>`/`<w:del>` around it, which is easy to do by accident and invisible in the accepted view. Wrap runs in `<w:ins>`/`<w:del>` with `w:id`, `w:author`, `w:date` attributes. Inside `<w:del>`, the text element is `<w:delText>`, not `<w:t>`. A deleted paragraph mark (`<w:pPr><w:rPr><w:del w:id=".." w:author=".." w:date=".."/></w:rPr></w:pPr>`) means "merge this paragraph into the next" — so deleting a paragraph outright is that plus a `<w:del>` around every run. The `<w:del/>` must come before the rPr's other children; their order is schema-enforced.

To produce a clean copy with all tracked changes accepted: `python scripts/accept_changes.py in.docx out.docx`.

Accepting a deleted paragraph mark should join that paragraph to the one below it, so a paragraph whose runs are *all* deleted vanishes. Word does this; `accept_changes.py` and `pandoc --track-changes=accept` don't always. Both fail the same way — they strip the deleted text but leave the emptied paragraph behind, which reads as a stray empty bullet when it was auto-numbered:

- `pandoc --track-changes=accept` never joins the paragraphs.
- `accept_changes.py` (LibreOffice) joins them correctly, except when the deleted paragraph is followed by an empty spacer paragraph.

An empty bullet in either view is an artifact of that view, not a defect in the document. Check paragraph deletions in the XML.

## Comments

Comments require six cross-linked files. Use the helper — directory mode when you'll also be editing `document.xml` (saves an unzip/rezip cycle), `.docx`-direct mode otherwise:

```bash
# Against an already-unpacked directory (preferred when also placing markers)
python scripts/comment.py unpacked/ "Fees & expenses cap is too low"
python scripts/comment.py unpacked/ "Agreed" --parent 0

# Against a .docx directly
python scripts/comment.py contract.docx "This cap is too low" -o annotated.docx
```

The script writes `comments.xml`, `commentsExtended.xml`, `commentsIds.xml`, `commentsExtensible.xml`, the relationships, and the content-type overrides. Comment IDs are auto-assigned. It then prints the `<w:commentRangeStart>`/`<w:commentRangeEnd>`/`<w:commentReference>` snippet to add to `word/document.xml` so the comment anchors to specific text — until you place those markers, the comment exists but is not visible.

## Dependencies

`docx` (npm, preinstalled — install only if `require('docx')` fails) · `pandoc` · LibreOffice (`soffice`) · `pdftoppm` (Poppler)

"""Render the per-page EMFs to PNG contact sheets (2 pages side by side) for review."""
from pathlib import Path
from PIL import Image

PAGES = Path(__file__).resolve().parent / "pages"
files = sorted(PAGES.glob("page-*.emf"))
rendered = []
for f in files:
    im = Image.open(f)
    im.load(dpi=72)
    im = im.convert("RGB")
    canvas = Image.new("RGB", im.size, "white")
    canvas.paste(im)
    rendered.append(canvas)

target_h = 1000
scaled = [im.resize((round(im.width * target_h / im.height), target_h)) for im in rendered]
for i in range(0, len(scaled), 2):
    pair = scaled[i : i + 2]
    sheet = Image.new("RGB", (sum(p.width for p in pair) + 30 * (len(pair) + 1), target_h + 60), (120, 120, 120))
    x = 30
    for p in pair:
        sheet.paste(p, (x, 30))
        x += p.width + 30
    name = PAGES / f"sheet-{i + 1:02d}.png"
    sheet.save(name)
    print(name.name, sheet.size)

"""Downscale the E2E screenshots for the user guide (540x1200 JPEG, light border)."""
from pathlib import Path
from PIL import Image, ImageOps

SRC = Path(__file__).resolve().parent.parent
OUT = Path(__file__).resolve().parent / "img"
OUT.mkdir(exist_ok=True)

SHOTS = {
    "signin": "e2e-01-signin.png",
    "home": "e2e-02-sam-list.png",
    "detail-approx": "e2e-03-sam-detail-before.png",
    "detail-exact": "e2e-04-sam-after-rsvp.png",
    "creator-actions": "e2e-07-avery-actions.png",
    "confirm-cancel": "e2e-08-confirm-dialog.png",
    "cancelled": "e2e-09-cancelled.png",
    "no-groups": "e2e-11-taylor.png",
    "live-walk": "e2e-12-live-2.png",
    "create": "e2e-13-create.png",
    "edit": "e2e-14-edit.png",
}

for name, file in SHOTS.items():
    image = Image.open(SRC / file).convert("RGB")
    image = image.resize((540, 1200), Image.LANCZOS)
    image = ImageOps.expand(image, border=2, fill=(214, 221, 216))
    image.save(OUT / f"{name}.jpg", "JPEG", quality=86, optimize=True)
    print(f"{name}.jpg {image.size} {(OUT / f'{name}.jpg').stat().st_size // 1024} KB")

# Environment update

The user guide is finished: a 15-page Word document, saved as [docs/Altair_Meetups_User_Guide.docx](docs/Altair_Meetups_User_Guide.docx) and committed (`c3fc50b`).

It's written for people using the app and for evaluators running it. Each section is short and task-based:
- signing in and out
- groups and meetups
- RSVP, with the approximate area versus the exact meeting point
- creating, editing and cancelling a meetup
- the live walk demo
- a privacy table showing who can see what
- what the app's messages mean, and troubleshooting
- setup steps for evaluators
- the demo accounts (Appendix A)

The 11 screenshots come from today's run on the emulator against your hosted backend, plus two I captured for the Create and Edit screens without saving anything. I retook the groups screenshot as Riley on Riverside so your test meetup "Xxx" doesn't appear. The cover uses your app's park artwork and green colours, and there's a linked table of contents with page numbers.

I checked the layout by having Word render every page and fixed what I found:
- The contents page listed itself.
- Every section started on a new page, leaving mostly blank pages (20 pages before, 15 now).
- The footer page totals counted the cover; the exported PDF now reads "Page 1 of 14" through "Page 14 of 14".

One thing I couldn't run is the docx skill's own file validator, because a Python package it needs isn't installed. Word opened the file, filled in the contents and saved it without errors.

The screenshots show Expo Go's grey gear button; the guide says in one line that it isn't part of the app.

I saw you committed your `GroupPicker` / `MeetupListScreen` changes in the meantime (`1d8995f`). The working tree is clean, nothing is pushed, and the emulator, API server and Expo are still running.

"""Report page-break / keep settings in the guide, and what precedes each section heading."""
import re
import sys
import zipfile

xml = zipfile.ZipFile(sys.argv[1]).read("word/document.xml").decode("utf8")
print("pageBreakBefore (on):", len(re.findall(r"<w:pageBreakBefore(?: w:val=\"(?:true|1|on)\")?/>", xml)))
print("pageBreakBefore (off):", len(re.findall(r"<w:pageBreakBefore w:val=\"(?:false|0|off)\"/>", xml)))
print("keepNext:", len(re.findall(r"<w:keepNext", xml)), " keepLines:", len(re.findall(r"<w:keepLines", xml)))
print("cantSplit rows:", len(re.findall(r"<w:cantSplit", xml)))
print("explicit page breaks:", len(re.findall(r'w:type="page"', xml)))
print("lastRenderedPageBreak (Word's own markers):", len(re.findall(r"lastRenderedPageBreak", xml)))

# Paragraphs that carry keepNext: show their text
paras = re.findall(r"<w:p[ >].*?</w:p>", xml, flags=re.S)
def text(p):
    return "".join(re.findall(r"<w:t[^>]*>([^<]*)</w:t>", p))
for p in paras:
    if "<w:keepNext" in p and "drawing" not in p:
        t = text(p)
        if t and not t[:2].strip().isdigit() and not t.startswith("Appendix"):
            print("  keepNext on non-heading:", t[:70])

p('Altair Meetups helps members of small neighborhood walking groups plan dog walks together. Any member can post a meetup with a title, a start time and a public meeting place. Other members of the same group can see it, say they are going (RSVP) and find the meeting point on a map.'),
  p('Meetups are private to their group. People outside a group see nothing about its meetups, and the exact meeting point is shared only with the people who are actually coming.'),
  h2('What you can do'),
  ...bullets([
    '**Browse your groups** and their upcoming meetups, soonest first.',
    '**Open a meetup** to see when and roughly where it is, who is hosting and who is going.',
    '**RSVP** to reveal the exact meeting point, and **withdraw** if your plans change.',
    '**Create a meetup** for one of your groups.',
    '**Edit or cancel** a meetup you host.',
    'Try the **Live walk (demo)** map, which animates simulated walkers.',
  ]),
  h2('Who this guide is for'),
  p('Sections 2 to 12 are for anyone using the app. Section 14 is for evaluators and developers who need to run the app and its server on their own machine.'),

  // 2
  h1('2. Getting started'),
  h2('What you need'),
  ...bullets([
    'An Android phone or emulator with **Expo Go** (SDK 58) installed. iOS works too.',
    'An Altair account. For trying the app, use one of the demo accounts in **Appendix A**.',
    'A running Altair server and app build. If someone shared the app with you, this is already done; otherwise see Section 14.',
  ]),
  p('The screenshots in this guide were taken in Expo Go on Android. The round gear button that appears on them belongs to Expo Go’s developer tools, not to Altair.', { run: { italics: true, color: C.muted, size: 20 } }),
  h2('Key terms'),
  ...table(
    ['Term', 'Meaning'],
    [
      ['Group', 'A neighborhood walking group. You can belong to several groups, or none.'],
      ['Meetup', 'A planned walk in one group: a title, a start time and a meeting point.'],
      ['Host', 'The member who created a meetup. Only the host can edit or cancel it.'],
      ['RSVP', 'Saying you are going. It adds you to the attendee list and reveals the exact meeting point.'],
      ['Approximate area', 'A circle of about 400 m around (but not centered on) the meeting point, shown before you RSVP.'],
    ],
    [2300, CONTENT - 2300],
  ),

  // 3
  h1('3. Signing in and out'),
  p('Altair signs you in with your email address and password.'),
  ...steps([
    'Open the app. The **Welcome back** screen appears.',
    'Enter your **Email** and **Password**. Tap the eye icon to show or hide the password.',
    'Tap **Sign in**. Your groups and meetups load.',
  ]),
  ...callout('Demo accounts', [
    'Under **Try a demo account**, tap a face (Avery, Jordan, Sam, Riley, Taylor) to fill in that email address. You still type the password; see Appendix A.',
  ]),
  ...figures([['signin', 'The sign-in screen with demo accounts']]),
  h2('Signing out'),
  p('Tap the **sign-out icon** at the top right of the meetups screen. Your session ends on this device and cached meetup data is cleared, so the next person who signs in cannot see it.'),
  p('If you see **"That email and password don’t match an account."**, check both fields and try again.'),

  // 4
  h1('4. Your groups and meetups'),
  p('After signing in you see **Your groups** and the **Upcoming meetups** of the selected group.'),
  ...steps([
    'Tap a group card to select it. A check mark shows which group is selected.',
    'Scroll **Upcoming meetups**. They are listed **soonest first**, and cancelled meetups stay in the list, clearly marked.',
    'Pull down on the list to refresh it.',
    'Tap a meetup to open its details.',
  ]),
  ...figures([
    ['home', 'Groups and upcoming meetups'],
    ['no-groups', 'A member who is not in any group yet'],
  ]),
  h2('Reading a meetup card'),
  ...table(
    ['Part of the card', 'What it tells you'],
    [
      ['Date tile and time', 'When the walk starts, in your device’s time zone.'],
      ['Location line', 'The exact place name if you are going or hosting; otherwise “Approximate area · RSVP to see the spot”.'],
      ['Status badge', '**Scheduled** or **Cancelled**.'],
      ['Your meetup / You’re going', 'Shown when you host the meetup or have RSVP’d.'],
      ['Going count', 'How many members have RSVP’d.'],
    ],
    [2800, CONTENT - 2800],
  ),
  p('If a group has no meetups yet, you see **No meetups yet** with a button to create one. If you do not belong to any group, the app tells you so; a group member has to add you first.'),

  // 5
  h1('5. Meetup details'),
  p('The details screen shows everything you are allowed to see about a meetup:'),
  ...bullets([
    'The title, date and start time, status, and who is hosting.',
    'The **Meeting point** map: an approximate area or the exact point (see Section 6).',
    '**Who’s going**: the names of members who have RSVP’d.',
    'The actions available to you: RSVP, withdraw, and for the host, edit and cancel.',
  ]),
  p('Pull down to refresh. If the meetup cannot be loaded, you see a message with a **Try again** button.'),

  // 6
  h1('6. RSVPs and the meeting point'),
  h2('Before you RSVP: an approximate area'),
  p('Until you RSVP, the map shows a shaded circle of about 400 m. The meeting point is somewhere inside it, but the circle is deliberately **not centered** on it, and the place name is hidden. This is enough to decide whether a walk is near you.'),
  h2('After you RSVP: the exact meeting point'),
  p('Tap **RSVP — I’m going**. The map immediately switches to a pin on the exact meeting point, the place name and coordinates appear, and you are added to **Who’s going**. You do not need to sign out or restart the app.'),
  ...figures([
    ['detail-approx', 'Before RSVP: approximate area'],
    ['detail-exact', 'After RSVP: exact meeting point'],
  ]),
  ...callout('Why the exact spot is hidden until you RSVP', [
    'A meetup says where a neighbor will be at a specific time, often early or late and alone with a dog. Sharing the exact spot only with people who are actually coming keeps that information with the people who need it. The host always sees the exact point of their own meetup.',
  ]),
  h2('Withdrawing an RSVP'),
  ...steps([
    'Open a meetup you are going to.',
    'Tap **Withdraw RSVP**.',
    'You see “Your RSVP was withdrawn.” You leave the attendee list and the map returns to the approximate area.',
  ]),
  h2('When you cannot RSVP'),
  ...bullets([
    '**Cancelled meetups** accept no new RSVPs. If you were already going, you can still withdraw.',
    '**Meetups that have started** accept no new RSVPs.',
    'RSVPing twice is harmless; you are only listed once.',
  ]),

  // 7
  h1('7. Creating a meetup'),
  ...steps([
    'On the meetups screen, select the group and tap **Create new meetup**.',
    'If you belong to more than one group, choose the **Group** at the top of the form.',
    'Enter a **Title**, for example “Saturday morning loop”.',
    'Set the **Date and start time**. It must be in the future.',
    'Under **Meeting point**, enter the **Place name** of a public place, then tap the map to drop a pin (drag it to adjust) or type the **Latitude** and **Longitude**.',
    'Tap **Create meetup**. The new meetup opens with a confirmation, and your group can see it straight away.',
  ]),
  ...figures([['create', 'The New meetup form']]),
  h2('Rules the app checks'),
  ...table(
    ['Field', 'Rule'],
    [
      ['Title', 'Required; 1 to 80 characters. Spaces at the start and end are removed.'],
      ['Date and start time', 'Required; must be later than now.'],
      ['Place name', 'Required; 1 to 120 characters. Use a public place, never a home address.'],
      ['Latitude / Longitude', 'Required; latitude −90 to 90, longitude −180 to 180.'],
      ['Group', 'Must be one of your groups. You are always recorded as the host.'],
    ],
    [2600, CONTENT - 2600],
  ),
  p('If something is wrong, the message appears next to the field. The server checks the same rules again, so a meetup can never be saved with invalid details.'),

  // 8
  h1('8. Editing a meetup (hosts)'),
  p('Only the host can edit a meetup, and only while it is scheduled. Other members do not see the **Edit meetup** button.'),
  ...steps([
    'Open your meetup and tap **Edit meetup**. The form opens with the current details.',
    'Change the title, start time or meeting point.',
    'Tap **Save changes**. You return to the meetup with “Changes saved.”',
  ]),
  ...figures([['edit', 'Editing a meetup you host']]),
  ...bullets([
    'A new start time must still be in the future.',
    'The group and the host cannot be changed.',
    'If you move the meeting point, members who have not RSVP’d see a new approximate area around the new spot.',
    'Cancelled meetups cannot be edited.',
  ]),

  // 9
  h1('9. Cancelling a meetup (hosts)'),
  p('Only the host can cancel a meetup. Cancelling is final: a cancelled meetup cannot be reopened.'),
  ...steps([
    'Open your meetup and scroll to **Cancel meetup**.',
    'Tap **Cancel meetup**. A dialog asks you to confirm.',
    'Tap **CANCEL MEETUP** to confirm, or **KEEP IT** to go back.',
  ]),
  ...figures([
    ['creator-actions', 'Host actions'],
    ['confirm-cancel', 'Confirming the cancellation'],
    ['cancelled', 'A cancelled meetup'],
  ]),

- Every content page is 85–100% full.
- The few pages with more space end just before the intentional page breaks (the contents page, the evaluator section, the appendix) or are the last page.
- The largest empty gap inside any page is about 7%.
- The page numbers run from 1 to 11 of 11.

The biggest remaining gap is about 15% at the bottom of page 6, where the three cancellation screenshots move together to the next page. I left it that way so the three-step sequence stays in one row.

# Engineering notes: Altair group meetups

**Scope.** The database, write layer, shared contract and React Native app for group meetups,
RSVPs and the meetup map, built from the provided schema starter, seed and feature spec. Both
optional bonuses are included.

**Status.** Verified against hosted Supabase (89 hosted tests), offline against the real
migrations on Postgres 17 (224 tests), and end to end on an Android emulator with Expo Go. Run
instructions are in [README.md](README.md); the evidence is in [QA_REPORT.md](QA_REPORT.md).

| Section                                                           | What it answers                                         |
| ----------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------- |
| [1. Product decision](#1-product-decision-approximate-area-until-rsvp) | The open question in the spec, and why                  |
| [2. Architecture](#2-architecture)                                | How the slice is put together                           |
| [3. Security model](#3-security-model)                            | Where each access rule is enforced                      |
| [4. What I would refuse to build first](#4-what-i-would-refuse-to-build-first) | The refuse-first item                                   |
| [5. Pushback on the spec](#5-pushback-on-the-spec)                | What I would change in the spec                         |
| [6. How this was built](#6-how-this-was-built-direction-and-review) | What was directed, what was caught, what I reviewed     |
| [7. Verification](#7-verification)                                | How the claims above are proven                         |
| [8. Trade-offs and next steps](#8-trade-offs-and-next-steps)      | What I would change for production                      |
| [9. Assumptions](#9-assumptions)                                  | Where the spec was silent                               |
| [10. Setup notes](#10-setup-notes)                                | Boot time, what slowed it, environment details          |

---

## 1. Product decision: approximate area until RSVP

**Decision.** Members who have not RSVP'd see an approximate area: a 400 m circle whose center is
offset from the meeting point, with a generic label instead of the place name. The creator and
members who have RSVP'd see the exact point and its name. RSVPing switches the map at once;
withdrawing switches it back.

**Why, in terms of the people using the app.** A meetup post says where a specific neighbor will
be at a specific time, usually early in the morning or in the evening, often alone with a dog.
Walking groups are "a handful to a few dozen neighbors" and membership is loose: people join, move
away, lose interest. "Everyone in the group" is therefore a wider and less known audience than
"the people who said they are coming". The decision a non-attendee actually makes, _is this walk
near me, and when_, needs only the area and the time. The exact spot is needed only by the people
who will walk there, and an RSVP is a light but visible commitment (attendees are listed by name),
which gives the host accountability for who knows the spot. The cost is one tap before seeing the
pin; the area is precise enough to decide whether to tap.

**How the area is computed** (in the database, `app.approximate_area`):

- **Offset, not centered.** The center is the exact point moved 120–280 m in a random direction;
  the radius is 400 m. The exact point is always inside the circle, so the area is honest.
- **Computed once and stored.** It is never re-randomized per request, so repeated reads cannot be
  averaged back to the spot. If the host moves the point (bonus edit), a new area is computed for
  the new point.
- **Random per meetup.** A fixed shift or grid would let anyone who RSVPs to one meetup learn the
  offset for all of them. A grid snap was also rejected because a spot near a cell's center yields
  an area centered almost exactly on the spot.
- **Place name withheld.** "North gate, Linden Park" pins the spot as precisely as coordinates, so
  it never leaves the server before RSVP; the app shows its own label.

**Where it is enforced.** The exact point lives in its own table, `meetup_meeting_points`, whose
row-level security policy admits only the creator and attendees who are still group members. RLS
is per row, not per column, so this split is what lets the database alone withhold the location;
the `meetups` row any member can read contains only the area. The service applies a second,
independent check (`meetingPointFor`), and every response is parsed through the shared schema,
which drops any field the contract does not declare.

## 2. Architecture

```
 Expo app (React Native) ──HTTPS + member JWT──▶ Fastify API (Node 22) ──▶ Supabase Postgres
 screens → hooks → gateway ports                 routes → services → ports ← repositories
           │                                     (parse with the shared Zod contract)
           └── sign-in only ──▶ Supabase Auth ◀── token verification
                         packages/shared: one Zod contract, imported by the API and the app
```

| Layer          | Server                                                        | App                                             |
| -------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------- |
| Presentation   | `http/` (app, auth hook, error handler), `features/*/routes`  | `features/*/screens`, `components`, `ui/`       |
| Application    | `features/*/…service.ts` (rules, no SQL)                      | `features/*/hooks.ts` (React Query)             |
| Domain / ports | `domain/` (types, ports, pure rules, errors)                  | `core/ports.ts`                                 |
| Infrastructure | `infrastructure/` (SQL repositories, unit of work, verifier)  | `core/api`, `core/supabase`; wiring in `App.tsx` |

Dependencies point inward, and `index.ts` / `App.tsx` are the only composition roots. That is what
lets the same services run against fakes, embedded Postgres and hosted Supabase, and lets the app
screens be tested with fake gateways. A mechanical check found no import cycles across the 70
source files.

**Key choices**

- **One contract.** Request and response schemas live in `packages/shared`. The app validates with
  them for immediate feedback; the server validates with them authoritatively. Request schemas are
  strict, so an extra `createdBy` is a 400 rather than silently ignored.
- **Writes can only go through the API.** This is enforced by the database, not by convention
  (see §3).
- **Reads also go through the API**, although the database is built so that direct reads would be
  safe (the hosted tests prove it). One contract for everything means a meetup's viewer flags and
  meeting-point view are computed in one place.
- **Deliberately small.** One Fastify process, plain SQL in three repositories, no ORM, no DI
  container, no event bus. Plain SQL is easier to review against RLS policies than generated
  queries.

## 3. Security model

| Rule                                                    | Enforced by                                                                                 |
| ------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Outsiders read nothing (meetups, attendees, locations)  | RLS on every table, via membership predicates                                               |
| Exact point only for the creator and attendees          | RLS on `meetup_meeting_points`; service check; response schema                              |
| Home location never exposed                             | Column-level grant: client roles may read only `id, display_name` from `users`             |
| Every write passes server-side Zod validation           | `authenticated` (the role a member's JWT maps to) has **no** write grants                  |
| Creator-only cancel and edit                            | RLS update policies for the writer role                                                     |
| RSVP only for yourself, only in your own group          | RLS insert/delete policies + membership trigger                                             |
| No RSVP to a cancelled or started meetup                | Trigger, with a `FOR SHARE` row lock that serializes it against a concurrent cancel         |
| Cancellation is final; identity columns immutable       | Update trigger                                                                              |
| A changed start time must be in the future (edit bonus) | Zod schema + update trigger                                                                 |

**How the API acts as a member.** After verifying the token with Supabase Auth and validating the
body, the API runs each request in a transaction with `SET LOCAL ROLE` (`authenticated` for reads,
`altair_api_writer` for writes) and a transaction-local `request.jwt.claims`. RLS therefore
applies exactly as for the member's own query, and a pooled connection never carries one member's
identity into the next request. `altair_api_writer` is a `NOLOGIN` role that PostgREST cannot
switch to, so the app cannot reach it.

**No information in errors.** An outsider gets the same `404 Meetup not found` for a real meetup
as for a random id (tested byte for byte). The RSVP trigger checks membership before status, so an
outsider cannot probe whether a meetup is cancelled. Unknown errors become a generic 500; SQL and
stack traces are only logged server-side, and the `Authorization` header is redacted from logs.

**Service-role key.** Not used anywhere and not in any `.env` template.

| Privileged function                                                                           | Security                  | Why it is safe                                                                                  |
| --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `app.is_group_member`, `is_meetup_member`, `can_see_exact_meeting_point`, `shares_group_with` | DEFINER, `search_path=''` | Read memberships without recursing into their RLS; answer yes/no about the caller only.         |
| `app.guard_rsvp_insert` (trigger)                                                             | DEFINER                   | Locks the meetup row; returns nothing but an error code; checks membership first.               |
| `app.on_meeting_point_update` (trigger, edit bonus)                                           | DEFINER                   | Fires only for rows the caller's RLS already allowed them to update; recomputes the area.       |
| `app.can_join_live_walk` (Realtime bonus)                                                     | DEFINER                   | Same audience as the exact point, and only while the meetup is scheduled.                       |

## 4. What I would refuse to build first

**Live location sharing of members during walks.** For a dog-walking group, a walk usually starts
at someone's front door, so a live track leaks the very home location this spec makes private,
along with routines and the times a person is out. I would not build it until there is per-walk
opt-in, sharing that starts only inside a geofence around the public meeting point and stops
automatically, no retention of tracks, and visibility limited to the attendees of that walk. The
Realtime bonus is scoped accordingly: synthetic positions only, on private channels that only the
host and attendees can join.

## 5. Pushback on the spec

1. **Meetups have no end time or duration.** "Started" is the only cut-off, so nothing is ever
   "past"; lists grow forever and the app cannot separate upcoming from past walks.
   _Recommendation:_ add a duration and default the list to upcoming.
2. **Cancelling or editing notifies nobody.** A 7 a.m. walk cancelled without anyone hearing about
   it is a real failure mode, and moving the meeting point after people RSVP silently changes their
   plans. _Recommendation:_ cancellation and location-change notifications should be the first
   follow-up, ahead of anything else on the roadmap.
3. **A creator who leaves the group orphans the meetup.** RLS requires membership, so they can no
   longer cancel it. _Recommendation:_ define ownership transfer or a group-admin role.
4. **The attendee list is visible before RSVP.** Reasonable inside a small group, but combined with
   the time and area it tells members who will be where. _Recommendation:_ make this a conscious
   product decision rather than a default.
5. **A fixed 300 m minimum is the wrong measure.** It protects little in dense areas and may still
   identify the spot in sparse ones where a circle contains one plausible public place.
   _Recommendation:_ express the requirement as ambiguity (how many plausible places the area
   contains), not meters.

## 6. How this was built: direction and review

The repository was built with an AI coding agent (Claude Code) under my direction, in sessions
whose exported log accompanies the submission. The agent ran every command reported in
QA_REPORT.md.

### What I directed

From my instructions in the session:

- **The product decision** (§1): members who have not RSVP'd see only an approximate area of at
  least 300 m that is not centered on the point; the creator always sees the exact point.
- **The stack and environment:** Expo React Native, a Fastify TypeScript API, Zod, and hosted
  Supabase rather than Docker; a portable Node 22 in the project folder rather than changing the
  system install.
- **Clean, feature-based architecture** with ports and adapters and no unnecessary abstraction.
- **Strict compliance with the starter README:** migrations through the Supabase CLI, the starter
  applied exactly once, no reset of the hosted database without my approval.
- **Security expectations:** RLS for every rule, no service-role shortcuts, home location never
  exposed, writes only through the validated API.
- **Testing and honesty rules:** tests against real authenticated sessions; nothing marked as
  passed unless it ran; unresolved issues reported, not hidden.
- **Git discipline:** history preserved, milestone commits, no history rewriting, nothing pushed
  without my approval.
- **Scope and order:** mandatory requirements first and verified, then the edit bonus, then the
  Realtime bonus.
- **A suspected authorization defect** (a non-creator editing a meetup), which I raised for
  investigation; see below.
- **The mobile redesign** (commits `a661d8d`, `1d8995f`) was committed by me in a separate session.

### What the process caught and corrected

| Issue                                                                                                                                     | How it was found                                     | Resolution                                                                                         |
| ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `npm run server` crashed on startup although every test passed: Node loaded the shared package as CommonJS                                | Starting the real server                             | Shared package declared ESM; a regression test now starts the real entry point (`9e227bb`, `11606fd`) |
| Testing Library 14 made `render` and `fireEvent` asynchronous; app tests were not rendering anything                                      | 18 of 23 app tests failed on first run               | Tests await them; a lint rule now rejects floating promises in app tests                           |
| Two React rules-of-hooks violations                                                                                                       | Code review while writing                            | Fixed before the first run                                                                         |
| A mutation-test restore missed an untracked file, leaving a permissive RLS policy on disk                                                 | Checking the result of the restore                   | Policy restored by hand; a search confirms no permissive policy remains                            |
| A "dry run" of the migrations really applied them: PowerShell strips a bare `--`                                                          | The command's output                                 | It reached the intended, verified-empty project; added `npm run db:push:dry` and a README warning  |
| A `react-native` version pin followed a transient tool result                                                                             | The tool later reported the opposite                 | Corrected in a follow-up commit, not rewritten (`103443d` → `6871c72`)                             |
| Reported: a non-creator could edit a meetup                                                                                               | My report                                            | No defect: in the hosted database only the creator's update changes rows. The real gap was test coverage, so DB-level hosted tests were added (`e1b4b7d`) |
| A meetup whose creator left the group would vanish from lists (inner join)                                                                | Code review                                          | Left join with "Former member"                                                                     |

The privacy tests were checked by breaking what they protect: weakening the exact-point policy and
the service check made 12 tests fail; weakening the edit policy made its test fail.

### My own review and hand changes

> **To be completed by me before submission.** Only I can state this accurately; nothing here has
> been written on my behalf.
>
> - What I reviewed line by line, and what I checked by running it myself:
> - What I changed by hand, and why:
> - Where I disagreed with or overruled the agent:

## 7. Verification

| Evidence                                                                                                                          | Result               |
| --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | -------------------- |
| Offline: shared contract, server unit tests, API and database tests on the real migrations and seed (PGlite, Postgres 17), app tests | 224 passed           |
| Hosted Supabase: real Auth tokens, API suite, direct PostgREST bypass attempts, RSVP-versus-cancel race, edit authorization        | 89 passed            |
| On-device journey (Android emulator, Expo Go, hosted backend): approximate → RSVP → exact → withdraw; host cancel; outsider        | Passed, step by step |
| `npm run demo:privacy`: outsider and non-RSVP results through the API and directly through Supabase                               | As specified         |

The four roles from the brief (outsider, member without RSVP, member with RSVP, creator) and the
multi-group member (Riley, in both groups) are covered, including the map data per group. The
offline harness is a faithful Postgres, not Supabase: Auth, PostgREST, Realtime and the pooler are
covered only by the hosted suite.

## 8. Trade-offs and next steps

- **Least-privilege connection.** The API connects with the database owner's credentials and drops
  privileges per transaction. For production I would use a dedicated login role that is a member of
  only `authenticated` and `altair_api_writer`.
- **Token verification** calls Supabase Auth per request: simple, and correct for revoked sessions
  and both key types. At scale I would verify locally against the project's JWKS.
- **Area size** is a constant 400 m; it should eventually depend on place density (§5, item 5).
- **Randomness:** the offset uses `random()`, drawn once and unobservable; `gen_random_bytes` would
  be stricter.
- **Not yet built:** rate limiting, pagination (keyset on `starts_at, id`), notifications, and
  measured performance of the live map (no FPS, latency or battery figures are claimed; see
  [REALTIME_MAP_BONUS.md](REALTIME_MAP_BONUS.md)).

## 9. Assumptions

- A member may RSVP to their own meetup; it only adds them to the attendee list.
- RSVPing twice returns 200 and leaves one RSVP, even if the meetup has since been cancelled or
  started. Withdrawing without an RSVP is a 200 no-op.
- Cancelling an already-cancelled meetup is a 200 no-op. A host may cancel a meetup that has
  started.
- A member who leaves a group loses access to its meetups, including exact points they saw via RSVP.
- "Started" means `starts_at <= now()` on the database clock, which the app and the trigger share.
- Deleted users appear as "Former member".

## 10. Setup notes

- **Boot time.** Migrations, seed and a seed sign-in took minutes once the connection string was
  right. Two things slowed it down: the dashboard's direct connection host is IPv6-only and
  unreachable from an IPv4 network (the Session pooler string works), and the pooler string is
  shown with a literal `[YOUR-PASSWORD]` placeholder that must be replaced.
- **Environment.** No Docker was used, so only the hosted path was exercised. Expo SDK 58 needs
  Node ≥ 22.13; a portable, checksum-verified Node 22 lives in the git-ignored `.tools/` folder.
- **If the starter was already applied** through the SQL editor, `db push` would try to apply it
  again and fail. Mark only the starter as applied, then push the rest:

  ```bash
  npx supabase migration repair --db-url "$DATABASE_URL" --status applied 20261001000000
  npm run db:push
  ```

| Rule                                                    | Enforced by                                                                                 |

  again and fail. Mark only the starter as applied, then push the rest:

  ```bash

  npm run db:push
  ```

offset from the meeting point, with a generic label instead of the place name. The creator and
members who have RSVP'd see the exact point and its name. RSVPing switches the map at once;
withdrawing switches it back.

**Why, in terms of the people using the app.** A meetup post says where a specific neighbor will
be at a specific time, usually early in the morning or in the evening, often alone with a dog.
Walking groups are "a handful to a few dozen neighbors" and membership is loose: people join, move
away, lose interest. "Everyone in the group" is therefore a wider and less known audience than
"the people who said they are coming". The decision a non-attendee actually makes, _is this walk
near me, and when_, needs only the area and the time. The exact spot is needed only by the people
who will walk there, and an RSVP is a light but visible commitment (attendees are listed by name),

  and both key types. At scale I would verify locally against the project's JWKS.

  measured performance of the live map (no FPS, latency or battery figures are claimed; see

## 9. Assumptions

- A member may RSVP to their own meetup; it only adds them to the attendee list.
- RSVPing twice returns 200 and leaves one RSVP, even if the meetup has since been cancelled or
  started. Withdrawing without an RSVP is a 200 no-op.
- Cancelling an already-cancelled meetup is a 200 no-op. A host may cancel a meetup that has
  started.
- A member who leaves a group loses access to its meetups, including exact points they saw via RSVP.
- "Started" means `starts_at <= now()` on the database clock, which the app and the trigger share.
- Deleted users appear as "Former member".

## 10. Setup notes

- **Boot time.** Migrations, seed and a seed sign-in took minutes once the connection string was
  right. Two things slowed it down: the dashboard's direct connection host is IPv6-only and
  unreachable from an IPv4 network (the Session pooler string works), and the pooler string is
  shown with a literal `[YOUR-PASSWORD]` placeholder that must be replaced.
- **Environment.** No Docker was used, so only the hosted path was exercised. Expo SDK 58 needs
  Node ≥ 22.13; a portable, checksum-verified Node 22 lives in the git-ignored `.tools/` folder.
- **If the starter was already applied** through the SQL editor, `db push` would try to apply it
  again and fail. Mark only the starter as applied, then push the rest:

  ```bash
  npx supabase migration repair --db-url "$DATABASE_URL" --status applied 20261001000000
  npm run db:push
  ```

Confirmed: `.tools\node22` holds Node 22.23.4, and the folder in your command doesn't exist. Run these in the same PowerShell window:

```powershell
$env:PATH = "D:\altar\.tools\node22;$env:PATH"
node --version          # must print v22.23.4 before you continue
cd D:\altar\mobile
npx expo start --clear  # then press "a" for the Android emulator
```

I start Expo with `npx expo start --clear` from the `mobile` folder because PowerShell strips the `--` in `npm run mobile -- --clear`. That's the same problem that hit the migration dry run, so `--clear` never reached Expo.

For the API server, open a second PowerShell window and set the PATH again, because the change only applies to that one window:

```powershell
$env:PATH = "D:\altar\.tools\node22;$env:PATH"
cd D:\altar
npm run server
```

If you'd rather not set the PATH in every new window, install Node 22 or later system-wide from nodejs.org (LTS). After that, plain `npm run mobile` and `npm run server` work anywhere.

aiTitle: ALTAIR meetup access, RSVP, and map privacy

content.text: The date has changed. Today's date is now 2026-10-30. No need to announce the new date — the user's own clock shows it.

RSVP comes from the French *"répondez s'il vous plaît"*, "please reply". In everyday use it means telling an organizer whether you're coming to an event.

In Altair, RSVPing means tapping **"RSVP — I'm going"** on a meetup. That does three things:
- **Adds your name to "Who's going"**, so the host and the group can see you're coming.
- **Reveals the exact meeting point**: the place name and the pin on the map. Before you RSVP, you only see an approximate area of about 400 m.
- **Gives you access to the Live walk demo** for that meetup.

If your plans change, **Withdraw RSVP** removes you from the list, and the map goes back to the approximate area.

You can't RSVP to a meetup that has been cancelled or has already started. If you RSVPed before it was cancelled, you can still withdraw.

## Troubleshooting

- **`npm ci` or Expo complains about the Node version**: Expo SDK 58 needs Node ≥ 22.13.
- **npm 10 crashes with `Cannot read properties of null (reading 'edgesOut')`**: a known npm 10
  arborist bug with this workspace; npm 11 works (`npx npm@11 ci`).
- **`db push` cannot connect**: use the _Session pooler_ string (IPv4); check Database → Network
  restrictions; percent-encode special characters in the password (`@` → `%40`). `--dry-run`
  shows what would be applied without changing anything.
- **`db push` says a migration was already applied / the starter's tables exist**: the starter was
  applied some other way (e.g. pasted in the SQL editor). Never apply it twice; see
  ENGINEERING_NOTES.md → "If the starter was already applied".
- **App shows "App is not configured"**: `mobile/.env` is missing or incomplete; restart
  `npm run mobile` after editing it (`npx expo start -c` clears the cache).
- **App shows "Could not reach the server"**: `EXPO_PUBLIC_API_URL` is not reachable from the
  device (see the table above), or the API is not running.
- **Expo Go says the project is incompatible**: install Expo Go for SDK 58.

## Submitting as an archive

The history must travel with the code. Either zip the folder **including `.git`** (exclude
`node_modules`, `.tools` and `.env` files), or create a single-file bundle that `git clone` can read:

```bash
git bundle create altair.bundle --all     # recipient: git clone altair.bundle altair
```

content.text:
An emulator is running now, but it isn't mine. Android Studio started its own copy (`emulator @altair_pixel`), and my 4 GB cold boot was shut down when that happened. Android Studio's launch **resumed the old 2 GB snapshot** again, so you're back to the same memory starvation that froze Expo Go.

I'll stop here rather than fight Android Studio over the emulator while you're using it. Please do this once from Android Studio:

1. Open **Device Manager** and stop **altair_pixel**: the ■ button, or just close the emulator window.
2. In the same row, open the **⋮** menu and choose **Cold Boot Now**.

A cold boot ignores the old snapshot and uses the saved 4 GB setting. From then on, normal launches keep 4 GB, because the snapshot gets re-saved at 4 GB.

Then reopen the app in Expo Go. It'll find your running Metro server at `exp://10.0.2.2:8081`.

If you'd prefer, tell me and I'll do it instead: stop the emulator, delete the stale snapshot, and cold-boot it at 4 GB. Either way, once it's up I can confirm it really has 4 GB before you start recording.

Yes, the steps are correct for Sam. **Saturday morning loop is the card just above "Weeknight short walk"**. It has only scrolled up out of view. You can see its bottom edge in your screenshot: "Approximate area · RSVP to see the spot", **Scheduled**, and the two faces with **"2 going"** (Jordan and Riley).

To get it back:
- **Swipe down inside the "Upcoming meetups" list** (on the cards, not on the group card above). That list scrolls on its own, so the header and group card stay put while the meetups move.
- Then tap **Saturday morning loop** and follow the steps.

It's always first because meetups are sorted soonest first: Saturday is on Thu 5 Nov, Weeknight on Sun 8 Nov.

For recording, make the emulator window taller. At its current size the meetups list only fits about one and a half cards, so you'll be scrolling a lot on camera.

"""Count secret-like strings in the exported AI session log, without printing any of them."""
import re
import sys

patterns = {
    "Supabase secret key (sb_secret_)": r"sb_secret_[A-Za-z0-9_-]{10,}",
    "Supabase publishable key (sb_publishable_)": r"sb_publishable_[A-Za-z0-9_-]{10,}",
    "JWT / access token (eyJ...)": r"eyJ[A-Za-z0-9_-]{20,}\.[A-Za-z0-9_-]{20,}\.[A-Za-z0-9_-]{10,}",
    "Postgres URL with a password": r"postgres(?:ql)?://[^\s:@\"'<>]+:(?!\*\*\*\*|\[YOUR-PASSWORD\]|YOUR-DB-PASSWORD|x@|p@|y@)[^\s@\"'<>]{4,}@",
}
path = sys.argv[1]
text = open(path, encoding="utf8", errors="replace").read()
print(f"{path}: {len(text) // 1024} KB")
for name, pattern in patterns.items():
    print(f"  {name}: {len(re.findall(pattern, text))} match(es)")

entries.name: Monitor
entries.description:
Start a background monitor that streams events from a long-running script. Each stdout line is an event — you keep working and notifications arrive in the chat. Events arrive on their own schedule and are not replies from the user, even if one lands while you're waiting for the user to answer a question.

Pick by how many notifications you need:
- **One** ("tell me when the server is ready / the build finishes") → use **Bash with `run_in_background`** and a command that exits when the condition is true, e.g. `until grep -q "Ready in" dev.log; do sleep 0.5; done`. You get a single completion notification when it exits.
- **One per occurrence, until the monitor expires (re-arm to continue)** ("tell me every time an ERROR line appears") → Monitor with an unbounded command (`tail -f`, `inotifywait -m`, `while true`).
- **One per occurrence, until a known end** ("emit each CI step result, stop when the run completes") → Monitor with a command that emits lines and then exits.

Your script's stdout is the event stream. Each line becomes a notification. Exit ends the watch.

  # Each matching log line is an event
  tail -f /var/log/app.log | grep --line-buffered "ERROR"

  # Each file change is an event
  inotifywait -m --format '%e %f' /watched/dir

  # Poll GitHub for new PR comments and emit one line per new comment
  last=$(date -u +%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ)
  while true; do
    now=$(date -u +%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ)
    gh api "repos/owner/repo/issues/123/comments?since=$last" --jq '.[] | "\(.user.login): \(.body)"'
    last=$now; sleep 30
  done

  # Node script that emits events as they arrive (e.g. WebSocket listener)
  node watch-for-events.js

  # Per-occurrence with a natural end: emit each CI check as it lands, exit when the run completes
  prev=""
  while true; do
    s=$(gh pr checks 123 --json name,bucket)
    cur=$(jq -r '.[] | select(.bucket!="pending") | "\(.name): \(.bucket)"' <<<"$s" | sort)
    comm -13 <(echo "$prev") <(echo "$cur")
    prev=$cur
    jq -e 'all(.bucket!="pending")' <<<"$s" >/dev/null && break
    sleep 30
  done

**Don't use an unbounded command for a single notification.** `tail -f`, `inotifywait -m`, and `while true` never exit on their own, so the monitor stays armed until timeout even after the event has fired. For "tell me when X is ready," use Bash `run_in_background` with an `until` loop instead (one notification, ends in seconds). Note that `tail -f log | grep -m 1 ...` does *not* fix this: if the log goes quiet after the match, `tail` never receives SIGPIPE and the pipeline hangs anyway.

**Script quality:**
- Every pipe stage must flush per line or matches sit in its buffer unseen: `grep` needs `--line-buffered`, `awk` needs `fflush()`. `head` cannot flush at all — `| head -N` delivers nothing until N matches accumulate, then ends the stream.
- In poll loops, handle transient failures (`curl ... || true`) — one failed request shouldn't kill the monitor.
- Poll intervals: 30s+ for remote APIs (rate limits), 0.5-1s for local checks.
- Write a specific `description` — it appears in every notification ("errors in deploy.log" not "watching logs").
- Only stdout is the event stream. Stderr goes to the output file (readable via Read) but does not trigger notifications — for a command you run directly (e.g. `python train.py 2>&1 | grep --line-buffered ...`), merge stderr with `2>&1` so its failures reach your filter. (No effect on `tail -f` of an existing log — that file only contains what its writer redirected.)

**Coverage — silence is not success.** When watching a job or process for an outcome, your filter must match every terminal state, not just the happy path. A monitor that greps only for the success marker stays silent through a crashloop, a hung process, or an unexpected exit — and silence looks identical to "still running." Before arming, ask: *if this process crashed right now, would my filter emit anything?* If not, widen it.

  # Wrong — silent on crash, hang, or any non-success exit
  tail -f run.log | grep --line-buffered "elapsed_steps="

  # Right — one alternation covering progress + the failure signatures you'd act on
  tail -f run.log | grep -E --line-buffered "elapsed_steps=|Traceback|Error|FAILED|assert|Killed|OOM"

For poll loops checking job state, emit on every terminal status (`succeeded|failed|cancelled|timeout`), not just success. If you cannot confidently enumerate the failure signatures, broaden the grep alternation rather than narrow it — some extra noise is better than missing a crashloop.

**Output volume**: Every stdout line is a conversation message, so the filter should be selective — but selective means "the lines you'd act on," not "only good news." Never pipe raw logs; filter to exactly the success and failure signals you care about. Monitors that produce too many events are automatically stopped; restart with a tighter filter if this happens.

Stdout lines within 200ms are batched into a single notification, so multiline output from a single event groups naturally.

The script runs in the same shell environment as Bash. Exit ends the watch (exit code is reported). Every monitor expires after `timeout_ms` (default 5 minutes, at most 30 minutes): it is killed and you get one notice with the event count. Re-arm it if you still need the watch; for a long watch (PR monitoring, log tails) set `timeout_ms` to the maximum and re-arm on each expiry, and widen the filter if an expiry with no events was unexpected. Use TaskStop to cancel early.
**ws source** — open a WebSocket and stream each incoming text frame as an event. No shell, no polling: the server pushes, you get notified.

  Monitor({
    ws: {url: 'wss://events.example.com/stream', protocols: ['v1']},
    description: 'deploy events',
  })

Each text frame becomes one notification (multiline frames stay as one event). Binary frames are reported as `[binary frame, N bytes]` rather than passed through. Socket close ends the watch with the close code surfaced; errors are surfaced before close. Same rate limiting as bash — a firehose will be suppressed and eventually stopped, so subscribe to a filtered feed where one exists.

Prefer this over `command: 'websocat wss://…'` — it avoids the extra process and line-buffering pitfalls. Use bash when you need to transform or filter frames with shell tools before they become events.

description.description: Short human-readable description of what you are monitoring (shown in notifications).

timeout_ms.description: Kill the monitor after this deadline. Default 300000ms. Deadlines above 1800000ms are capped to 1800000ms. You are notified at expiry and can re-arm.

command.description: Shell command or script. Each stdout line is an event; exit ends the watch.

ws.description: WebSocket to open. Each text frame is an event; binary frames are reported as a placeholder line. Socket close ends the watch. Cannot be combined with command.
